 Medicare enrollment calls spur new tools for seniors 
 By Wade DeVinney / Special to the Fairfax County Times 
 Nov 20, 2026 
 3 hrs ago

 Those annoying, incessant phone calls older adults get daily during Medicare open enrollment have created unexpected market opportunities for some entrepreneurs. 
 During the Medicare open enrollment period, many older people are inundated with phone calls from companies trying to convince them to switch Medicare plans, even if the person receiving the call is not actively enrolled in Medicare. As a result of the confusion and frustration these calls create, some entrepreneurs and nonprofit leaders have developed tools allowing people who want Medicare to ignore the phone calls altogether.  
 One of those entrepreneurs is Mike Boshardy, who is a licensed Medicare regulatory attorney in Illinois. He had grown tired of people giving seniors bad advice on Medicare and wanted to create a platform with as objective advice as possible. So in 2024, he created  The Pocket Protector , a free-to-use site which assesses the user’s needs and recommends a plan based on an algorithm. 
 “I envisioned a [tool] where these products are actually competing based on which one is the best, rather than which one is putting the most dollars towards marketing or which one is putting the most dollars towards commission.” 
 The issue, according to Boshardy, is that when companies cold-call a senior citizen to sell them a Medicare plan, they are motivated less to find the best plan for the customer and more to sell the plan that will cover the cost of the telemarketer and other business operations. 
 “If you’re in a call center-style environment, you’ve got to pay for the time of a licensed agent on the phones,” Boshardy said. “The rule of thumb is that the lead you’re talking to to get a client on the phone is going to cost you $50, the agent’s time is going to cost you $50 and the overhead is going to cost you $50. When you’re paying for conversations at a $150 clip, it’s pretty impossible to tell somebody to stay in their current plan or to sign up for a plan that you don’t get  paid on .” 
 The Pocket Protector is free for the end user, and the company makes its money through commissions from the providers of the plans it recommends. But because Boshardy’s company does not incur the costs associated with call centers, he can afford to routinely recommend plans that are best for the user but will not earn him a commission. Boshardy estimates that roughly 25% of the recommendations  The Pocket Protector makes do not earn him any commission. 
 “We’ve spent two years building technology to be able to actually provide  people these  unbiased opinions,” Boshardy said. 
 The Pocket Protector is not the only resource looking to ease the confusion of Medicare open enrollment season.  SeniorNavigator , a nonprofit based in Richmond, connects senior citizens with organizations to address specific problems and publishes advice on open enrollment. Fairfax County also has a dedicated office for older adults, providing resources for aging citizens.  
 This year, technology has worked out in The Pocket Protector’s favor in new ways. According to Boshardy, more seniors than ever are using his service after consulting with ChatGPT or another AI chatbot. 
 “One of the great things about seniors relying on robots to help them shop is robots are not susceptible to traditional sales pressure,” Boshardy said. “They’re not going to get rushed, they’re not going to get flustered, they’re not going to feel emotionally like they have to enroll in something.” 
 Medicare open enrollment this year is particularly frustrating for more people than usual since 10% of Medicare Advantage enrollees lost coverage. Last year,  Investopedia reported  that Medicare insurance provider Humana was dropping roughly 600,000 Medicare Advantage enrollees from their plans after 2026. In fact,  according to a study by Johns Hopkins University economist Dr. Mark Meiselbach , 2.9 million Americans who were enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan now have to find a new plan for 2027. 
 Providers such as Humana typically decline to renew Medicare plans when they determine that their current enrollment rate is no longer profitable. 
 “The r esults of this study show that, in 2026, approximately one in 10 beneficiaries in HMO or PPO Medicare Advantage plans will be forced to disenroll from their current plan due to their plan exiting the market,” Meiselbach wrote in his study. “Drivers of higher plan exit may include changes to plan payments and risk adjustment, as well as unanticipated increases in health care use among Medicare Advantage enrollees.” 
 The Medicare open enrollment period lasts until Dec. 7.
